questions.q: What is the primary textual evidence used to establish Yashodhara's impatience with superficial art appreciation in the opening paragraph?
questions.a: The author describes Yashodhara becoming restless ("व्याकुल") and speaking sharply ("तीक्ष्ण स्वर") when visitors treat her paintings as mere decoration. A wrong answer like "she smiled politely" reveals the student cannot distinguish between the author's narration and the character's actual reaction, indicating a failure to identify direct characterization.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the author considers Yashodhara's blending of traditional techniques with modern sensibility as her defining artistic trait.
questions.a: The author values this blend because it represents a living tradition — Yashodhara uses ancient mineral pigments and folk motifs but composes them with contemporary spatial awareness, making heritage relevant without fossilizing it. A wrong answer focusing only on "she uses old colours" shows the student misses the synthesis aspect, treating tradition and modernity as separate rather than integrated.

questions.q: The author writes: "उसकी कला में लोक का सौन्दर्य और शास्त्र की गहराई दोनों हैं।" Identify two specific moments in the text where Yashodhara demonstrates folk aesthetics (लोक सौन्दर्य) and two where she demonstrates classical discipline (शास्त्र की गहराई).
questions.a: Folk aesthetics: (1) using village women's tattoo patterns as border motifs, (2) depicting festivals with communal spontaneity. Classical discipline: (1) preparing canvas with 14-layer traditional ground, (2) adhering to iconometric rules for deity proportions. A wrong answer listing only themes (e.g., "she paints villages") without technical specifics shows the student cannot distinguish subject matter from artistic method.

questions.q: Compare how the author's portrayal of Yashodhara's authority differs when she teaches students versus when she negotiates with gallery owners. What does this contrast reveal about her character?
questions.a: With students she is nurturing but exacting ("हाथ पकड़कर सिखाती, पर गलती पर डाँटती"), while with gallery owners she is firm yet diplomatic ("मूल्य नहीं घटाती, पर प्रदर्शनी की शर्तें मान लेती"). This contrast reveals her core integrity — she compromises on presentation but never on artistic standards. A wrong answer saying "she is strict with both" misses the nuanced power dynamics, showing inability to analyze contextual behaviour.

questions.q: The author claims Yashodhara "revitalised a dying tradition." Evaluate this claim using three pieces of evidence from the text, considering both artistic innovation and social impact.
questions.a: Evidence: (1) Artistic — she introduced natural binder recipes that prevented cracking in humid climates, (2) Social — trained 12 women from her village as professional artists, (3) Institutional — her works entered the National Museum's permanent collection. The claim is valid because innovation addressed material decay while training ensured generational continuity. A wrong answer citing only "she became famous" reveals evaluative superficiality — confusing recognition with substantive revitalisation.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Yashodhara's perspective on the day the author visited her studio, reflecting her inner conflict between preserving purity and reaching wider audiences.
questions.a: A strong entry: "Today a city writer watched me grind lapis lazuli. He asked why I don't use synthetic blue. I wanted to shout — this stone carries centuries of prayers! But then he smiled at my Ganesha's curved trunk... maybe sharing the soul matters more than guarding the pigment." A weak entry describing only external events ("He came, saw paintings, left") shows inability to infer interiority from textual gaps.
